transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: Researchers at Oxford University have developed a new type of malaria vaccine that has shown unprecedented effectiveness in early trials, raising hopes for finally controlling one of the world's deadliest diseases. Malaria kills more than 400,000 people every year, mostly children under five years old in sub-Saharan Africa, and efforts to develop an effective vaccine have been ongoing for decades with limited success. The new vaccine, which targets the malaria parasite at multiple stages of its life cycle, was found to be about 80 percent effective at preventing severe malaria in young children during phase 2 trials. Researchers say this is significantly more effective than any previous malaria vaccine. The vaccine works by combining several different antigens—proteins from the parasite—to trigger a stronger and broader immune response than earlier vaccines. Larger phase 3 trials involving thousands of children are now planned, and if those are successful, the vaccine could be widely available within five to seven years. Scientists caution that the vaccine won't eliminate malaria entirely, but combined with other measures like bed nets and insecticides, it could dramatically reduce deaths and illness from the disease.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: The state of California has approved a new law requiring all new cars sold in the state to be zero-emission electric vehicles by 2035, marking one of the most ambitious climate policies in the United States. The rule, which was announced by the California Air Resources Board, will phase out gasoline-powered cars gradually, with intermediate targets requiring that 35 percent of new cars sold be electric by 2026 and 68 percent by 2030. California is the largest car market in the United States and the fifth largest in the world, so the rule is expected to have a major impact on the auto industry globally, pushing manufacturers to accelerate their transition to electric vehicles. Several other states have already said they will adopt California's standards, meaning the rule could affect more than a third of the U.S. auto market. Supporters say the move is necessary to fight climate change and reduce air pollution, which causes thousands of premature deaths every year. Critics, however, argue that the transition will be too expensive for many consumers and that the state isn't building enough charging infrastructure fast enough to support all the electric vehicles.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A team of archaeologists in Turkey has discovered the remains of a previously unknown ancient city that dates back more than 5,000 years, making it one of the oldest urban settlements ever found in the region. The city, located in southeastern Turkey near the border with Syria, was discovered during excavations for a new highway project. Researchers have found the foundations of large buildings, streets, defensive walls, and thousands of artifacts including pottery, tools, and jewelry. The size and complexity of the settlement suggest that it was an important political and economic center in its time, with a population of possibly several thousand people. Archaeologists say the city was part of the early Bronze Age civilization that flourished in the region, and its discovery could change our understanding of how cities first developed in the ancient Near East. The excavation has been temporarily halted while archaeologists work to document and preserve the site, and the highway project may be rerouted to avoid destroying the ancient remains.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Jennifer): Hey Mike, what are you doing here at the community center? I didn't know you volunteered here.
Man (Mike): Oh, hey Jennifer. Yeah, I come here every Saturday morning to help with the after-school program for kids. I help them with their homework and play games with them. It's really fun.
Woman: That's awesome! I had no idea you volunteered. What made you start doing that?

Man: Well, I used to be really busy with my job and everything, but then I realized I was spending too much time just sitting around watching TV and scrolling through my phone on weekends. I wanted to do something more meaningful with my time. And I've always liked working with kids, so this seemed perfect.
Woman: That's really cool. I've been thinking about volunteering too, but I don't know where to start. There are so many organizations, and I'm not sure what I'd be good at.
Man: What are you interested in? Do you like working with kids, or would you prefer something else?
Woman: I'm not sure. I do like kids, but I also care about environmental stuff. And I like animals too. There's just too many options— I don't know how to choose.

Man: Well, you don't have to commit to just one thing forever. You could try a few different things and see what you like best. A lot of organizations are happy to have occasional volunteers, not just regular ones.
Woman: That's true. But what if I'm not good at it? I'd feel bad if I showed up and was useless.

Man: Oh, don't worry about that! Most volunteer work doesn't require special skills—they just need people who are willing to show up and help. And they'll train you for whatever you need to do. When I first started here, I had no idea what I was doing, but the other volunteers showed me the ropes.
Woman: Hmm, okay. How much time do you spend volunteering? I work full-time, so I don't have a ton of free time.
Man: I come here for about three hours every Saturday morning. That's it. It doesn't have to be a huge time commitment. Even a couple hours a month makes a difference.
Woman: That's not bad at all. Do you know of any environmental volunteer opportunities around here? I think I might want to try that first.

Man: Yeah, actually! There's a local environmental group that does park clean-ups and tree planting on weekends. They're always looking for more volunteers. And there's also the animal shelter—they need people to walk dogs and play with the cats.
Woman: Both of those sound good. How do I sign up?
Man: I can give you the contact information for both groups. Or if you want, you could come with me next Saturday to help with the kids first, just to see what volunteering is like. No pressure.
Woman: That might be a good way to start. Let me think about it and I'll let you know. Thanks for all the info, Mike. It's really inspiring that you do this.
Man: No problem! I think you'd love it. It's actually really rewarding—you get way more out of it than you put in.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (George): Hey Chloe, how's your new job going? You started at the marketing agency last month, right?
Woman (Chloe): It's going... okay, I guess. It's not exactly what I expected, honestly.
Man: Oh no, what's wrong? I thought you were excited about it.

Woman: I was excited! The job sounded perfect—marketing for a creative agency, good pay, nice office... But the reality is different. The work is really boring, mostly just data entry and making spreadsheets. I thought I'd be working on creative campaigns and coming up with ideas, but I'm basically just doing administrative work.
Man: That sounds disappointing. Have you talked to your manager about it? Maybe they don't realize you want more creative work.

Woman: I mentioned it once, but she said that everyone starts out doing this kind of work and that I'll get to do more interesting stuff after I've been there a while. But I don't know—some people have been there for years and they're still doing the same boring work.
Man: Hmm, that's tricky. How are your coworkers? Are they nice at least?

Woman: They're okay, but everyone works really long hours and seems stressed out all the time. People are there until 7 or 8 PM almost every night, and even on weekends sometimes. I thought the work-life balance would be better. I'm already exhausted, and I've only been there a month.
Man: That sounds really tough. What are you going to do? Are you going to quit?

Woman: I don't know. I don't want to quit after only a month—that would look bad on my resume. And the pay is really good, which is nice. But I'm so unhappy there. I dread going to work every morning.

Man: I get that. But you know, your mental health is more important than a paycheck or what looks good on a resume. If it's really making you miserable, maybe you should start looking for something else. You don't have to quit first—you can look for other jobs while you're still there.
Woman: Yeah, you're right. But what if I can't find another job? The job market is pretty competitive right now.

Man: Well, you have a good degree and you're smart and hardworking. I'm sure you'll find something. And hey, even if the next job isn't perfect either, at least you'll know what you don't want. Every job teaches you something.

Woman: That's a good way to look at it. I guess I should start updating my resume and looking at job postings. I don't want to make a hasty decision, but I also don't want to stay somewhere that makes me miserable.
Man: Exactly. Take your time, but don't stay somewhere just because you feel like you have to. You deserve to enjoy your work.
Woman: Thanks, George. It helps to talk about it. I've been feeling really stuck lately.
Man: No problem. Let me know if you want help with your resume or anything. I've been through a few job changes, so I know what it's like.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The ancient Olympic Games were one of the most important events in the ancient Greek world, and they have left a lasting legacy that continues to this day with the modern Olympic Games. But the ancient Olympics were very different from the modern games in many ways.

The ancient Olympics were first held in 776 BC in Olympia, a small town in southern Greece, and they continued for nearly 1,200 years until they were abolished in 393 AD by the Roman Emperor Theodosius I, who considered them a pagan festival. Unlike the modern games, which are held every four years in different cities around the world, the ancient Olympics were always held in the same place—Olympia. And only free Greek men were allowed to compete; women, slaves, and foreigners were excluded. Married women weren't even allowed to attend the games as spectators, on penalty of death.

The games were held in honor of Zeus, the king of the Greek gods, and they were as much a religious festival as a sporting event. People came from all over the Greek world to watch and compete, and a truce was declared across all Greek city-states during the games so that people could travel safely to Olympia, even if their cities were at war with each other.

The events in the ancient Olympics were quite different from today. The first games had only one event—a short foot race of about 200 meters. Over time, more events were added, including longer races, wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and the pentathlon, which included running, jumping, wrestling, javelin throwing, and discus throwing. Unlike modern athletes, ancient athletes competed completely naked, which may seem strange to us today but was normal in Greek culture.

Winning an Olympic event was one of the highest honors a Greek man could achieve. Winners didn't get gold, silver, and bronze medals like today—instead, they received a wreath made of olive leaves. But the real reward was fame and glory. Olympic champions were celebrated as heroes in their home cities, and they often received gifts, tax breaks, and other privileges for the rest of their lives. Poets wrote songs about them, and statues were built in their honor.

The modern Olympic Games, which began in 1896, were inspired by the ancient Olympics, but they are very different in many ways. Yet some things remain the same: the spirit of competition, the pursuit of excellence, and the way the games bring people together from different places and backgrounds.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: For most of human history, people thought that the Earth was the center of the universe, with the sun, moon, planets, and stars all revolving around it. This geocentric model, as it's called, seemed obvious from everyday experience—after all, the sun appears to move across the sky, and we don't feel like we're moving. It took thousands of years for people to realize that the Earth actually revolves around the sun, and the story of that discovery is one of the most important in the history of science.

The idea that the Earth goes around the sun—called the heliocentric model—was actually first proposed by a Greek astronomer named Aristarchus of Samos around 270 BC, but his idea was mostly ignored and forgotten for nearly 2,000 years. The geocentric model, developed by the ancient Greek astronomer Ptolemy, became the accepted view, and it remained the standard for over 1,400 years.

It wasn't until the 16th century that a Polish astronomer named Nicolaus Copernicus revived the heliocentric idea. Copernicus spent decades studying the movements of the planets and developed a mathematical model that explained their movements much more simply if the sun was at the center instead of the Earth. He published his theory in a book called *On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres* in 1543, the year he died.

Copernicus's theory was controversial and slow to gain acceptance. Many people, including the Catholic Church, rejected it because it contradicted their religious beliefs and their understanding of humanity's place in the universe. The Church banned Copernicus's book and declared the heliocentric model heretical.

But evidence for the heliocentric model continued to grow. In the early 17th century, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei used the newly invented telescope to observe the skies, and he made several discoveries that supported Copernicus's theory. He saw that Jupiter had moons orbiting around it, proving that not everything orbits the Earth. He also observed the phases of Venus, which could only be explained if Venus orbits the sun.

Galileo's discoveries made the heliocentric model harder to ignore, but they also got him in trouble with the Church. He was put on trial for heresy and forced to publicly renounce his beliefs, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest.

Over time, however, the evidence became overwhelming, and the heliocentric model gradually became accepted by scientists and eventually by everyone. The story of how we learned that the Earth isn't the center of the universe is a reminder that scientific progress often requires challenging our most basic assumptions about the world.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges facing humanity today, and its effects are already being felt around the world. But while the problem can seem overwhelming, there are many things that individuals, communities, and governments can do to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and slow the rate of climate change.

One of the biggest sources of greenhouse gas emissions is the energy we use to power our homes, businesses, and transportation. Switching to renewable energy sources like solar, wind, and hydroelectric power instead of burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas is one of the most important steps we can take. Many countries are already investing heavily in renewable energy, and the cost of solar and wind power has dropped dramatically in recent years, making it competitive with fossil fuels in many places.

Transportation is another major source of emissions. Switching from gasoline-powered cars to electric vehicles, using public transportation, biking, walking, and reducing air travel can all make a big difference. Building more walkable and bikeable cities and improving public transit systems can help reduce the number of cars on the road.

What we eat also matters. Meat and dairy production, especially beef, is responsible for a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions, including methane from cows and the land use changes required for grazing and growing feed crops. Eating less meat, especially red meat, and eating more plant-based foods can reduce your carbon footprint significantly. Reducing food waste is also important—about a third of all food produced in the world is wasted, which means all the energy and resources that went into producing it are wasted too.

Individual actions are important, but they're not enough on their own. Government policies are essential for driving large-scale change. Carbon pricing, which puts a cost on emitting carbon, can encourage businesses and individuals to reduce their emissions. Regulations on vehicle emissions, power plant pollution, and building efficiency can also make a big difference. And investing in research and development of new clean technologies can help accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy.

It's also important to remember that climate change is already happening, and we need to adapt to the changes that are already unavoidable. This means building infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather, protecting coastal communities from rising sea levels, and helping farmers adapt to changing rainfall patterns and temperatures.

While the challenge of climate change is enormous, there is reason for hope. Renewable energy is growing faster than expected, electric vehicles are becoming more common, and public awareness and concern about climate change are at all-time highs. The choices we make in the next few decades will determine what kind of planet future generations inherit, and there's still time to avoid the worst effects of climate change if we act now.
